content.title: Highlights From the Launch of NASA’s Artemis II Moon Mission
content.text: Reporting from Kennedy Space Center in FloridaThe lunar journey begins.ImageThe Artemis II crew blasted off on their lunar journey from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Wednesday.Credit...Kenny Holston/The New York TimesA towering orange-and-white NASA rocket blasted off from Florida on Wednesday evening, lifting four astronauts toward space and transporting spectators’ imaginations to a future in which Americans may again set foot on the moon.As they did during the heyday of the Apollo program, which first put men on the lunar surface, spectators squeezed onto the beaches along Central Florida’s Space Coast. The crowds cheered when the powerful rocket launched into the clear sky at 6:35 p.m. Eastern time. It traveled eastward, over the Atlantic Ocean, on a journey that will take astronauts around the moon but not land there.“We have a beautiful moonrise and we’re headed right at it,” said Reid Wiseman, the NASA astronaut who is the commander of the mission, as the crew headed into space.Tens of thousands of excited spectators exclaimed and hugged along Cocoa Beach and surrounding communities as the rocket shot into the sky on a column of fire and a long white vapor trail.“The contrast against the blue sky was absolutely remarkable,” said Anthony Rodriguez, 35, of Orlando. “It’s just an unforgettable sight.”The flight aboard a spacecraft named Integrity is taking Mr. Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen on what is expected to be a round trip of more than 695,000 miles to clear a path for more exploration, a new lunar landing, eventually a sustained human presence on the moon, and journeys farther out into the solar system.ImageThousands of excited spectators watched as the rocket rose on a column of fire into the sky above Florida.Credit...Kenny Holston/The New York TimesThe last time astronauts traveled that far was Apollo 17, in December 1972.“After a brief 54-year intermission, NASA is back in the business of sending astronauts to the moon,” Jared Isaacman, the NASA administrator, said during a news conference after the launch.The mission, known as Artemis II, is the 21st century equivalent of Apollo 8, when NASA astronauts Frank Borman, James Lovell and William Anders captured the attention of the world. When they launched in December 1968, it was the first time that astronauts rode on top of the mighty Saturn V rocket.For that mission, instead of just a short test flight around Earth, the space agency audaciously decided to send the crew all the way to the moon and back, the first time humans reached another celestial body.While many were elated with the Artemis II mission and its progress, others shrugged or continued their Wednesday, oblivious to the countdown.In New York City, Maxime Kryvian, 37, a business owner, came to Times Square to see if any screens were broadcasting the launch. To his surprise and disappointment, none of them were.“I was expecting to see hundreds of people crowded around to watch the launch,” he said, listening to the broadcast through earphones as it played on his own phone screen.Mr. Kryvian said people had lost interest in space exploration. “We’ve lost a sense of shared achievement,” he said. “We keep looking at our small screens instead of the big one.”At Tom’s Watch Bar in downtown Houston — also known as Space City and the home of NASA’s mission control for human spaceflight missions — locals were slowly packing in, but not to watch the Artemis II astronauts fly to the moon. Instead, they were looking forward to watching the Houston Rockets later in the evening.During the launch, most of the televisions in the sports bar were tuned in to a Yankees-Mariners baseball game. A couple of the smaller screens showed NASA’s live broadcast of the mission.ImageThe Orion capsule is taking, from left, Jeremy Hansen, Victor Glover, Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch on what is expected to be a lunar round trip of more than 695,000 miles.Credit...Kenny Holston/The New York TimesDuring the news conference, Mr. Isaacman said he thought that when the rocket lifted off, “a lot of people would be paying attention. I suspect when some of the imagery starts to maybe come back from the moon, that’s going to further bring people into this story.”And at the beginning of his address to the nation on Wednesday night, President Trump congratulated NASA and the astronauts for the successful launch.“It was quite something,” he said. “These are brave people.”Mr. Trump then quickly changed the topic to the war with Iran.Like Apollo 8, Artemis II aims to check that the spacecraft can safely make the journey and keep its crew alive during trips to and from the moon. This particular mission will conclude with a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean on April 10.Unlike the Apollo astronauts, who were all white men, this mission sets a number of firsts: Mr. Glover of NASA will be the first Black man to venture into deep space and Ms. Koch of NASA will be the first woman to do so. Mr. Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency will be the first person on a moon mission who is not an American.Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada spoke with Mr. Hansen in a video call before the launch. “It fills me with pride, but it also sends a real message to Canadians,” Carney said in a clip posted on social media. Hansen added, “The fact we’ll be the second country in the world to send a human into deep space says a lot.”In the 1960s, NASA was racing to beat the Soviet Union to the moon. This time, it does not want to fall behind the space ambitions of China, which is aiming to land its astronauts on the moon by the end of 2030. But the goal is not to win the sprint. It is to establish a continuing presence on the lunar surface, building an outpost over the next decade.Mr. Isaacman, a billionaire entrepreneur who became the NASA administrator in December, has made major revisions to the Artemis program and rallied a work force that was battered by uncertainty and downsizing last year to focus on putting new footprints on the moon by the end of 2028.“It’s the opening act,” Mr. Isaacman said of Artemis II, and the lessons learned from this mission will be applied to the ones that follow.ImageThe Silva-Martinez family, who drove from Houston, observed the launch in Cape Canaveral, Fla.Credit...Cassandra Klos for The New York TimesDuring the countdown, leaks of helium and hydrogen that scuttled plans to launch in February and March did not recur. But other technical glitches did pop up.First, engineers resolved a problem with the rocket’s flight termination system, which destroys the rocket in the event that the crew capsule is ejected during flight. Then, late in the countdown, NASA said it was working on a problem with a battery in that crew capsule ejection system, but it concluded the problem lay with the sensor and not the battery itself.Those issues pushed back liftoff by 11 minutes.But then the engines ignited, lifted upward the 322-foot-tall rocket, weighing 5.75 million pounds, generating a low, loud rumble that rolled across East Central Florida.After liftoff, another technical glitch prevented mission controllers from hearing what the astronauts were saying even though the astronauts could hear the commands from the ground. Communications were restored after a few minutes.There was also an undisclosed problem with the spacecraft’s toilet, prompting the crew to plan to use “backup waste management capabilities” until it could be resolved.The first few hours in space were busy, with two firings of the upper stage of the rocket that placed the spacecraft in a large looping orbit that swung out more than 43,000 miles.The Orion spacecraft separated from the upper stage of the rocket. Mr. Glover manually flew the spacecraft, nudging it close to the discarded stage. That mimicked the maneuvers that will be used during later missions for docking with lunar landers.VideoCreditCredit...NASA, via Associated Press“That is a good-looking American flag,” Mr. Glover said after a maneuver brought the rocket stage with a painted flag on its side into view of the capsule’s docking camera.On Thursday, Orion will fire its engines to push it on a path toward the moon. On Monday, it will reach the moon and swing around, passing over the far side. The astronauts will spend hours making observations of the lunar surface, including portions of the far side that have never been seen by human eyes before.As it passes behind the moon, Artemis will set a distance record for the farthest that any humans have traveled from Earth: 252,799 miles, or 4,144 miles farther than the Apollo 13 astronauts traveled when they had to make an emergency return to Earth.Although the mission seemed to be mostly going well so far, most of the mission still lies ahead. “We will hold our celebration until this crew is under parachutes and splashes down off the west coast of the United States,” Mr. Isaacman said.Katrina Miller contributed reporting from Houston, Ashley Ahn and Stella Raine Chu from New York, Vjosa Isai from Toronto and Dan Simmons from Cocoa Beach, Fla.Before going to sleep, the astronauts have a few more tasks including putting away the space suits and troubleshooting the problem with toilet.4 tiny spacecraft have tagged along with Artemis II.ImageCubeSats secured inside NASA’s Orion stage adapter in preparation for the Artemis I launch Kennedy Space Center in Florida in 2021.Credit...NASAFour small satellites called CubeSats hitched a ride to space with Artemis II. Each is from an international partner of NASA, and they will soon be deployed into orbit around Earth. They will be used in experiments to help NASA and other space agencies better design future missions to deep space.TACHELES, operated by the German Aerospace Center, will test how electrical components fare while exposed to space radiation. The mission’s data will help engineers develop lunar vehicles.ATENEA, a satellite from Argentina, will demonstrate radiation shielding methods, test light-sensing devices and validate long-range communication techniques for deep space missions.K-RadCube from South Korea will measure the effects of space radiation on human beings at different heights within the Van Allen belts, the rings of high-energy particles that surround Earth. It will use a device designed to mimic human tissue.The Saudi Space Agency will also fly a satellite called the Space Weather CubeSat-1 to study space weather at different altitudes above Earth.In 2022, NASA’s Artemis I mission flew with 10 CubeSats on board, including the world’s tiniest lunar lander and a solar-sailing asteroid scout. But several of the science experiments experienced difficulties, like loss of communications and battery anomalies, and some failed altogether.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe proximity operations have concluded. The crew in their Orion capsule will move away from the upper stage , which then will be nudged onto a course to burn up in the atmosphere over the Pacific Ocean.How likely is it that Artemis II will collide with debris in space?ImageA view from the Orion spacecraft of Artemis I, 57,000 miles from Earth, on its way to the moon in 2022.Credit...NASANASA has had to grapple with many risks and unknowns as it prepares the astronauts of Artemis II for their journey around the moon. But one risk that the crew members will not have to worry much about is colliding with debris during their 10-day mission.It’s true that NASA considers orbital debris to be a major hazard for crewed space missions. At a rocket’s blistering speed of up to 22,000 miles per hour, a one-centimeter fleck of paint can inflict the same damage as a 550-pound object traveling 60 miles per hour on Earth. A 10-centimeter projectile would have an impact comparable to seven kilograms of TNT.And the Artemis II mission encountered the densest region of human-made debris shortly after it launched, said Carolin E. Frueh, an associate professor at Purdue University who researches space traffic management. There are well over 10,000 active satellites and more than 25,000 objects larger than 10 centimeters currently in Earth’s orbit.Such risks factor into NASA’s launch scheduling, and the agency’s flight planners block off brief periods of time for missions like Artemis II to avoid during launch windows. That’s because a piece of space debris might come too close to the rocket as it heads to space.“There’s quite a few more that we manage now,” Jeff Spaulding, a senior test director for the ground systems at the NASA Kennedy Space Center, said during a news conference on Tuesday, referring to these time slots. “We’re at about 156.”Still, unpredictable things happen. A piece of debris could collide with a satellite and create fragments, or a satellite could malfunction.That happened on Sunday, when a SpaceX Starlink satellite experienced an “anomaly.” LeoLabs, a space tracking company, called it a “fragment creation event” and detected more than 10 smaller objects near the satellite.In an update, SpaceX said the event “poses no new risk” to Artemis II. A NASA spokeswoman said the agency was aware of the incident and saw “no significant risk”Once the spacecraft leaves Earth’s immediate neighborhood en route to the moon, there are even fewer known objects to maneuver around.As it approaches the moon, the Orion capsule that carries the four astronauts will fly within about 4,000 miles above the surface. This is much farther away than the Apollo-era spacecraft, which orbited the moon at an altitude of about 70 miles.For an April 1 launch, Artemis II will also set the mark for the farthest that anyone has ever traveled from Earth — 252,799 miles, or about 4,000 miles farther than Apollo 13’s crippled spacecraft did during its emergency return to Earth.Staying at a higher altitude during the flyby also reduces even further an already minuscule risk of a collision with space debris around the moon.“The good thing is Orion is not entering low lunar orbit,” Dr. Frueh said, where there are more objects, like scientific and communication satellites launched by NASA, India, China and South Korea, in the moon’s orbit.While the risks to Artemis II are low, as NASA, other space agencies and private companies send more missions to the moon, more surveillance and data will be necessary to keep vehicles safe, Dr. Frueh said.“We have to know that we are blind in that region, and without doing something, we will just replicate what we have done in the near Earth, where there’s a lot of debris and it’s in everybody’s way,” she said.If you watch NASA’s ongoing video stream from inside the Artemis II Orion capsule, you’ll notice something unfamiliar in space: smartphones with cameras. The crew were allowed to carry the devices during the mission and they are using them to take pictures and, presumably, do other things too. The phones can be seen floating around the capsule, unbound by gravity. No case needed?AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe proximity operations demonstration in Earth orbit continues for the Artemis II mission. The astronauts are maneuvering their capsule around the upper stage of the rocket that carried them to space. The purpose of the demonstration is to show how Orion could move and dock with a future moon lander.As the capsule moved from facing the nose of the rocket to its side, something came into view. “That is a good-looking American flag,” said Victor Glover, the Artemis II pilot, as he looked through his docking camera.Some rejoiced in NASA’s return to the moon. Others had a regular Wednesday.VideoThe scene at Kennedy Space Center ahead of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket taking off from Launch Complex 39B to begin the Artemis II mission on Wednesday in Cape Canaveral, Fla.CreditCredit...Kenny Holston/The New York TimesWhen NASA launched its first crewed mission to the moon in more than 50 years on Wednesday, reactions among Americans ranged from the excitement of space enthusiasts to the nonchalance of casual observers. Some were oblivious.Thousands of people assembled hours before launch at the Cocoa Beach Pier, about 20 miles south of Kennedy Space Center in Florida. When the giant rocket carrying the Artemis II astronauts rose into the sky at 6:35 p.m. on a column of fire, watchers on the pier and the surrounding sand cheered and hugged.“The contrast against the blue sky was absolutely remarkable,” said Anthony Rodriguez, 35, of Orlando, Fla. “It’s just an unforgettable sight.”Patti Joblon-Clarke had claimed her spot on the beach after flying in on Tuesday from her home near New York City. She was there with her daughter, Emma, who lives in West Palm Beach, Fla.“It was my dream to see a launch since I was a little girl,” said Ms. Joblon-Clarke, 69, who said she loves all things space.At about the same time, in New York City, some of the people strolling about in Times Square did not seem keen on the news. While avoiding negative headlines, some had missed mention of the event altogether, like India Sanchez, 27, a nurse.“I see the news and all these horrible things are happening,” Ms. Sanchez said. “I’d rather just stay away" from it all, she said.Others unaware of the launch shared similar sentiments. Robert Brusch, 30, said the constant bombardment of negativity from the news wore him out, but called the lunar mission a silver lining.“The idea of going to the moon seems positive,” Mr. Brusch said. “Human progress,” he added.People watching the Artemis II launch on a display outside of the News Corp building in Manhattan, on Wednesday.Credit...Adam Gray/Getty ImagesMaxime Kryvian, 37, was one of the few who went to Times Square to see if any of the large screens were broadcasting the launch. He found advertisements instead.A space enthusiast since childhood, he was disappointed to see the lack of interest. As the broadcast played on his own phone screen, Mr. Kryvian said he believed that space exploration was one of the last common missions for humanity.“We’re all too focused on our own existence,” he said. “We’re too busy looking at our small screens and not at the big one.”Tom’s Watch Bar in downtown Houston — also known as Space City, and the home of NASA’s astronaut training center — was packed on Wednesday afternoon, but not for the launch. Instead, people were preparing to watch the Houston Rockets play against the Milwaukee Bucks. During the launch, most of the TVs were tuned to the Yankees-Mariners game. A couple of the smaller screens showed NASA’s live broadcast, and later switched to local news.True Anomaly Brewing Co., a space-themed bar in Houston that is owned by four NASA scientists, put up the livestream of the launch for a couple dozen customers.“We figured this would be a good spot to witness a historic moment,” said Victor Mejia, who noted that some people in the taproom weren’t paying attention during liftoff.10 days, four astronauts and just one bathroom.VideoFor the First Time, a Toilet Heads Into Deep SpaceThe Orion spacecraft will take four crew members and one commode around the moon and back as part of the Artemis II mission. In April 2025, National Geographic worked with NASA and filmed the astronauts at an Orion space capsule model in Houston.CreditCredit...Cassandra Klos for The New York TimesWhile in orbit around Earth, the Artemis II crew called down to the mission team on the ground to report a problem with their toilet.They noticed a blinking fault light that NASA’s associate administrator Amit Kshatriya called a “controller issue” in a news conference, one that would take some hours to troubleshoot, which appeared to have been achieved in part by midnight.This is the first time a real toilet has been installed on a mission into deep space. The Apollo missions that carried astronauts to the moon in the 1960s and 70s did not have a toilet, nor a designated bathroom area on board. Those crews used waste collection bags on their way to the moon. They left those bags on the lunar surface to reduce mass and contamination risk during their journey back to Earth.The setup for Artemis was planned to be a bit more dignified.Aboard the Orion capsule is a specialized toilet called the Universal Waste Management System. The door is on the floor, situated next to the hatch the astronauts use to enter the spacecraft.ImageA replica of the toilet for training at the Johnson Space Center.Credit...Cassandra Klos for The New York Times“We’re pretty fortunate as a crew to have a toilet with a door on this tiny spacecraft — the one place that we can go during the mission where we can actually feel like we’re alone for a moment,” Jeremy Hansen, a mission specialist on Artemis II from the Canadian Space Agency, said in a video.But how exactly will the three men and one woman of Artemis II go in space?“Very carefully,” Branelle Rodriguez, Orion’s vehicle manager, said in a NASA podcast.“First and foremost,” she added, “make sure you get in a good configuration.”Another interesting fact: It’s very loud inside the toilet.“You have to wear hearing protection when you’re in here,” Christina Koch, a mission specialist from NASA, said in a video recorded for National Geographic.In microgravity, there’s not much to hold you — much less your poop — down. Orion has handrails and foot tethers that keep the crew secure during a bathroom run. The toilet has a funnel attached to a hose for urine and a seat for solid waste. Automatic air flow, which helps reduce odor, pulls the waste away from the body and into separate storage containers.If for some reason the Artemis toilet can’t be fixed, the astronauts will collect their urine in bags. The crew can still use the toilet to go number two, though the air flow may not be functioning.During longer missions, like those aboard the International Space Station, astronauts recycle their liquid waste and process it back into drinkable water. But as Artemis II is only 10 days long, the crew will vent urine out of the spacecraft every day.Fecal waste will be stored in a collection container that is fitted with filters to control odor and gas buildup. That will be disposed of once the crew returns to Earth.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe Orion capsule just separated from the second stage of the rocket. “I see it, look at that, woo hoo!” said Victor Glover, the Artemis II pilot, referring to the second stage after his camera started working.VideoCreditCredit...NASA, via Associated PressAn 18-minute, six second engine burn successfully sent Artemis II into a high-Earth orbit. Next: the Orion spacecraft will separate from the upper stage of the Space Launch System rocket. Then the astronauts will maneuver Orion close to the upper stage, mimicking some of the operations that will be needed for docking with lunar landers in the future.At the top of his address to the nation from the White House on Wednesday night, President Trump congratulated NASA and the astronauts for the successful launch of Artemis II. “It was quite something,” he said. “These are brave people,” he said of the four astronauts, before sharply transitioning to discuss the war with Iran.ImageCredit...Doug Mills/The New York TimesPrime Minister Mark Carney of Canada said he spoke with President Trump this evening to congratulate him on the successful launch of Artemis II. The U.S.-Canada relationship has become tense during Trump’s second term, especially because of Trump’s tariffs and threats to annex Canada, but today the two leaders had a shared goal. During the call, they discussed “the value of cooperation in space,” Carney said.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAnd with that, the news conference has concluded.Lori Glaze said that far less hydrogen fuel leaked during the loading of propellants on Wednesday than during earlier fueling tests. She said they even finished tanking earlier than they planned.Does the public even know that NASA is sending astronauts back to the moon today? “I’m willing to bet right now that a lot of people do,” said Jared Isaacman, the NASA administrator. “We’ll only draw in their interest further as the mission proceeds.” ImageCredit...Kenny Holston/The New York TimesThe astronauts will be able to see a lunar eclipse from space! They will be able to observe the sun’s outer atmosphere, known as the corona. “It will be a pretty cool and unique opportunity,” said Lori Glaze, an acting associate administrator at NASA. “We’ll get some images down at some point.” AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe global space race is “a great way to mobilize the resources of a nation,” Mr. Isaacman said. “Competition can be a good thing. And we certainly have competition now.” The ground platform that held the Space Launch System rocket before it launched is expected to have some damage. During Artemis I, the rocket’s power blasted the doors off the elevators near the launch pad.“We do anticipate there will be some items that need to be replaced,” said Lori Glaze, a NASA acting administrator. “It’s a violent environment.” Lori Glaze, an acting associate administrator at NASA, and Norm Knight, the NASA flight operations director, said the crew will go ahead with plans to demonstrate the ability of the Orion spacecraft to maneuver around the rocket’s second stage.When will Artemis II reach the moon?ImageThe Silva-Martinez family, who drove from Houston to attend the launch, watching the Artemis II launch at Kennedy Space Center.Credit...Cassandra Klos for The New York TimesAfter a picture-perfect launch on Wednesday evening, Artemis II is one step closer to the moon. If the mission continues as planned, the Orion capsule will reach the moon in five days, by Monday night.The spacecraft will orbit 43,730 miles above Earth’s surface for about 24 hours on what NASA calls a high-Earth orbit. This wide, looping path provides time to check important systems aboard Orion, including life support and deep-space communications.The crew also plans to test Orion’s ability to execute docking maneuvers for future flights in the early hours of the flight.If any serious problems arise while Orion is still in Earth orbit, mission managers will bring the astronauts home.During this loop, the spacecraft’s engines will fire to give a final outward nudge. The capsule, which carries the four astronauts, will then leave Earth’s orbit and begin its journey to the moon on Thursday evening.It will take around three days for the capsule to enter what NASA calls the lunar sphere of influence, the point at which the moon’s gravity will be stronger than Earth’s. The crew will spend the day testing their orange spacesuits, equipped with new technology to help astronauts breathe for up to six days if the capsule depressurizes in emergency situations.On Monday, the astronauts will begin their study of the moon’s surface, which will include viewing parts of the far side that have never been seen by human eyes. At its closest, the spacecraft will still be more than 4,100 miles from the surface. The moon will be appear to be the size of a basketball held at arm’s length.Artemis II will reach a distance of 252,799 miles from Earth, the farthest that human beings have ever traveled from Earth — 4,144 miles farther than Apollo 13 was when it needed to swing around the moon for its emergency return to Earth.While the spacecraft heads to the moon, it will be on what is known as a “free return” trajectory. This path uses the moon’s gravity to swing the capsule directly back to Earth without needing to fire any of its engines. That means Orion could return to Earth even if there were a failure of the propulsion system.It will take around four days to make the journey back to Earth, where Orion is expected to splashdown in the Pacific Ocean on April 10.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAmit Kshatriya, the NASA associate administrator, said there is a “controller issue” with the toilet on the Orion capsule and would take a few hours to troubleshoot. “We’re just getting started,” he said when addressing that and some other glitches with the spacecraft.Kshatriya added that the mission’s next critical maneuver in orbit will go ahead as scheduled and Artemis II will “stay in space.”Jared Isaacman, the NASA Administrator noted the temporary communication problem with the spacecraft in orbit. They are back in touch with the ground and they’re working to determine the cause of the problem.VideoCreditCredit...NASA, via Associated PressIsaacman said that after 54 years, “NASA is back in the business of sending people to the moon.”NASA’s post-Artemis II launch news conference is underway. You can watch it in the video player above.A Houstonian named Brett who declined to give his last name at Tom’s Watch Bar said he grew up in Clear Lake, Texas, the location of NASA’s Johnson Space Center. He said he knew about the moon mission and watched some of the agency’s preparations earlier today.But “I’m here for the Rockets game tonight,” he said. Then he closed his tab and left the bar to head to the stadium.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTWhat China sees as NASA launches Artemis II.ImageA miniature model from Chang’e 6, China’s sixth robotic lunar exploration mission at the Beijing Sci-Fi Carnival last week.Credit...Adek Berry/Agence France-Presse — Getty ImagesChinese scientists are likely watching the Artemis II mission closely. The country has its own ambitions for the moon — it wants to land its astronauts there by 2030.This is the new space race between the two superpowers. And it’s a close one.Last week, the NASA Administrator, Jared Isaacman, said that China might land on the moon before the United States. Mr. Isaacman had previously noted that the United States did not have as much leeway as it did during the Apollo program, when “we had near infinite time to get to the moon compared to the Soviets.”In response, the agency has accelerated the Artemis program, seeking to fly the Space Launch System rocket more frequently in the years to come, and potentially landing astronauts on the moon twice in 2028.The Artemis II mission will conduct critical tests toward that goal, particularly proving that the Orion capsule is safe for astronaut travel in deep space.But some scientists in China’s space program have downplayed the notion that China and the United States are locked in a race to the moon. China’s first moon landing, they say, is expected to be on the near side of the moon, the relatively accessible hemisphere we can see from Earth. That’s where Apollo 11 landed in the 1960s.By contrast, NASA’s Artemis program wants to land astronauts near the moon’s South Pole, a place that may be rich in the frozen water resources that could aid longer-term missions on the moon and into even deeper space.NASA has resolved some communication issues with the spacecraft in orbit and we’re beginning to see some video footage of the solar panels and the blackness of space.NASA has concluded its live video coverage of the launch, but it continues to provide coverage of the flight — you just have to switch the channel. You can watch it here on YouTube. Expect a lot scenes of mission control at Johnson Space Center in Houston as well as periodic audio updates from the Integrity crew and NASA’s commentators. In about a half hour, NASA officials will host a news conference on the flight, and Times journalists will provide updates about what they have to say.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTArtemis II is now in a stable orbit after a 26-second engine burn by the second stage of the Space Launch System rocket. That raised the low point of the elliptical orbit to ensure the spacecraft will not re-enter the atmosphere.April 1, 2026Stella Raine Chu Reporting from Times SquareMaxime Kryvian, 37, a business owner, came to Times Square to see if any screens were broadcasting the launch. To his surprise (and disappointment), none of them were. “I was expecting to see hundreds of people crowded around to watch the launch,” he said, listening to the the broadcast through earphones as it played from his own screen in his pocket. When Orion swings back around Earth, the upper stage will fire again to stretch the high point of the elliptical orbit to 43,730 miles. The upper stage will then separate. The astronauts will practice flying the Orion spacecraft via manual control, approaching the discarded stage and then holding position.The solar panels that will provide power to the Orion spacecraft and its systems have successfully deployed.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAt Tom’s Watch Bar in downtown Houston — also known as Space City and the home of NASA’s primary astronaut training center — locals slowly packed the space on Wednesday. But they were not there to watch the Artemis II astronauts fly to the moon. Instead, they were pregaming for the Houston Rockets, who will play the Milwaukee Bucks this evening. During the launch, most of the TVs were tuned in to a Yankees-Mariners game. A couple smaller screens were streaming NASA’s live broadcast of the mission, then later switched to local news.After a picture-perfect launch, Orion and the astronauts have a lot of critical maneuvers coming up. First, Orion’s solar arrays need to deploy. Then, 49 minutes after liftoff, the second stage will fire for the first time to raise the lowest point of the elliptical orbit. Without that, Orion would reenter the atmosphere.ImageCredit...Kenny Holston/The New York TimesTens of thousands of excited watchers exclaimed and hugged on the Cocoa Beach Pier and its surrounding sand in Florida as the rocket shot into the sky above, trailing a ball of fire and a long white vapor trail.“The contrast against the blue sky was absolutely remarkable,” said Anthony Rodriguez, 35, of Orlando. “It’s just an unforgettable sight.”The core stage has fallen away. The Orion, still connected to the second stage, is coasting in an elliptical orbit. Over the next hour, the second stage will fire several times to put Orion is a highly elliptical orbit around Earth to allow time to test out critical systems before setting out toward the moon.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENT“We have a beautiful moonrise and we’re headed right at it,” Reid Wiseman, the Artemis II mission commander, said from the spacecraft as it ascended atop the rocket.Liftoff. A colossal tower of flame kicks the Space Launch System rocket from Launch Pad 39B. The side boosters of the rocket have now separated.ImageCredit...Kenny Holston/The New York TimesThe last time this happened, Artemis I in 2022, the launch took place in the dark. We’ve never seen what this rocket looks like flying in the day time.The news center here at the space center just emptied out as everyone heads outside to watch.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe final 10 minutes, which NASA calls “terminal count,” is controlled by a computer. A launch controller can halt the countdown if something doesn’t look right.The countdown has resumed. Counting down for 6:35 and 12 seconds p.m. Eastern time.“Full-send,” Reid Wiseman, the mission commander of Artemis II said, as he and his crewmates atop the Space Launch System confirmed they were ready to fly. Charlie Blackwell-Thompson, the NASA Artemis II launch director replied: “You take with you the heart of this Artemis team, the daring spirit of the American people and our partners across the globe, and the hopes and dreams of this generation. Good luck. Godspeed Artemis II. Let’s go.”I’m at the University of Toronto, which is hosting what seems to be the main Artemis launch viewing party. It might be the only viewing party in the city: more than half of a small meeting room at a campus library has been overtaken by broadcast television crews. Some people are sticking star-shaped notes with guesses of possible launch times on a wall. My guess: 7:03 p.m.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe launch team is working to set a definite launch time.Artemis II is a go for launch.ImageCredit...Kenny Holston/The New York TimesApril 1, 2026Stella Raine Chu Reporting from Times SquareTimes Square bustled with tourists and commuters ahead of the launch on Wednesday evening. Among them, Jane Cardona, 33, a server, said she was aware of the launch only because she has friends who live in Florida. She said otherwise she wouldn’t have known, as she tends to stay away from the news. “I try to stay clear of everything so I don’t spiral,” she said. To Cardona, the launch seemed “minimal” compared to other news events.The countdown clock is holding at 10 minutes as NASA works through some issues. Highlights From the Launch of NASA’s Artemis II Moon Mission - The New York Times The Space Launch System rocket, which is being used by Artemis II, is unusual in that Congress, frustrated when President Obama canceled an earlier return-to-the-moon program called Constellation, gave detailed specifications for what it wanted NASA to build. The pieces of S.L.S. are, in large part, a remix of components of the space shuttles.The core stage — the big orange part — was built by Boeing with engines left over from the space shuttle program.Northrop Grumman made the smaller boosters attached to the side of the core stage. Those, using solid rocket fuel, provide most of the thrust at liftoff and then drop away a couple of minutes later. They are longer versions of those that were used by the space shuttles.The second or upper stage of the rocket is known as the interim cryogenic propulsion system. United Launch Alliance, a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, built this stage, which is necessary for the final push needed to reach orbit. It is a modified version of the upper stage that U.L.A. used for its now-retired Delta IV vehicles.Lockheed Martin built the Orion capsule, where the astronauts are sitting. The service module — the cylindrical component below the capsule that houses the propulsion, communications and power systems — is the contribution of the European Space Agency to the Artemis program and was built by Airbus.While SpaceX and Blue Origin do not play a part in Artemis II, they will have a central role in future missions, building the landers that will take NASA astronauts to the moon’s surface.A year from now, during Artemis III, the Orion spacecraft is expected to practice docking with one or both of the landers in orbit around Earth. Attempts to land on the moon are planned for Artemis IV and Artemis V in 2028.Why won’t Artemis II land on the moon?ImageEdwin “Buzz” Aldrin photographed by Neil Armstrong as they walked across the surface of the moon on July 20, 1969.Credit...Neil Armstrong/NASA, via Associated PressNASA landed astronauts on the moon for the first time in 1969, and then five times more. So why is it that in 2026 NASA is talking about going back to the moon, but not landing on it?Landing people on the moon is difficult, and no one has done it since 1972.That’s because after Neil Armstrong stepped on the moon during Apollo 11, many Americans felt that the space race with the Soviet Union was won and that further lunar exploration was not worth the expense. In the decades since, NASA has focused on low-Earth orbit with the space shuttles and the International Space Station.But now the United States wants to go back to the moon (and China wants to go for the first time). President Trump made returning to the moon a priority during his first administration, and the program continued under President Biden.The moon is a logical place to send people, both as a place to explore scientifically, and as somewhere that could be mined for resources like frozen water for later space missions, and helium-3 for futuristic energy technologies.But, with a task as complicated as settling on the moon, it is smart not to try to do too many things at once, especially when human lives are at stake.Things have changed since humans last traveled as far as the moon in 1972. Current technology, especially computers, have advanced far beyond what was available during the Apollo era. Inevitably, something will not work exactly as designed, and it will be good to identify and fix those issues before attempting a landing.That’s part of the purpose of Artemis II.Also, NASA cannot land on the moon without a moon lander, and there is not one ready yet.SpaceX, Elon Musk’s company, has a contract to build such a spacecraft. So does Blue Origin, the space company started by Jeff Bezos, the founder of Amazon. Under the current schedule, NASA wants to attempt two landings 2028.The Artemis II contract went to older NASA contractors. Boeing, Northrop Grumman and United Launch Alliance built the pieces of the Space Launch System rocket that will launch today, and Lockheed Martin built the Orion capsule that the S.L.S. rocket carries.There’s another thing NASA needs before it can return people to the moon: new spacesuits for astronauts to wear while stepping out from the lander. The agency has planned live conversations with the crew throughout the mission, known as “downlinks.” The first is scheduled for 10:24 p.m. Eastern on April 2. NASA said it would also broadcast a separate livestream from cameras attached to the Orion spacecraft.A full list of coverage with dates and timing can be found on NASA’s website.
